title: Sound waves and hearing
examTip: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum, because there are no particles to vibrate. This is the key difference between sound and electromagnetic waves. Always say this clearly in exam answers.
introTips: Sound is a longitudinal wave. Particles in the medium oscillate parallel to the direction the wave travels.
Sound needs a medium (particles) to travel. It cannot travel through a vacuum.
The speed of sound depends on the medium. It is fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases.
Frequency sets the pitch. Amplitude sets the loudness.
Ultrasound (above 20,000 Hz) is used in medicine. It is safe, and it reflects off boundaries inside the body.
intro: You can hear a thunderclap from kilometres away. A doctor can scan your unborn sibling using sound waves. Ships map the ocean floor using sound pulses that bounce back. Sound is one of the most basic ways we interact with the world. The physics behind it is fascinating. Electromagnetic waves carry your Wi-Fi signal. But unlike them, sound needs something physical to travel through: particles bumping into each other. That single fact explains a lot. It is why space is silent. It is why sound travels faster through steel than through air. It also shapes how engineers design concert halls for perfect acoustics.

keyPoints.heading: Sound as a longitudinal wave
keyPoints.content: Sound is a mechanical, longitudinal wave. It is made by vibrating objects, such as a speaker cone, vocal cords or a drum skin. These push and pull the particles in the medium around them, again and again. This creates compressions and rarefactions that travel outward from the source. Compressions are regions of high pressure, where particles are pushed together. Rarefactions are regions of low pressure, where particles are spread apart. The particles oscillate parallel to the direction of travel. So sound is longitudinal. Sound needs particles to vibrate. So it cannot travel through a vacuum, where there are no particles to carry the wave. This is why there is no sound in space. It is why you could not hear an explosion on the Moon.
writeBullets: Sound is a mechanical longitudinal wave. Particles oscillate parallel to the direction of travel
Made by vibrating objects: a speaker cone, vocal cords, a drum skin
Creates compressions (high pressure) and rarefactions (low pressure) in the medium
Cannot travel through a vacuum. It needs a medium (particles) to carry the wave
No sound in space. There are no particles to pass on the vibrations

keyTerms.def: A wave where particle oscillation is parallel to the direction of travel; sound is the key example
A region of high pressure in a sound wave where particles are pushed together
A region of low pressure in a sound wave where particles are spread apart
A wave that requires a physical medium (particles) to travel — cannot travel through a vacuum

keyPoints.memTip: Sound = SLAM: Sound is a Longitudinal, hAs Medium. It cannot travel through a vacuum.
keyPoints.tutor_note: People often say sound 'travels through air molecules'. Better: sound is passed on by air molecules vibrating. The molecules themselves don't travel along with the wave.

keyPoints.heading: Speed of sound in different media
keyPoints.content: The speed of sound depends on the medium it travels through. It does not depend on the frequency or amplitude. The key rule: sound travels fastest through solids, slower through liquids and slowest through gases. In solids, particles are closest together, with the strongest forces between them. So they pass on vibrations very efficiently. In gases, particles are far apart and interact weakly. So vibrations spread more slowly. Approximate speeds: steel ~5000 m/s, water ~1500 m/s, air ~340 m/s. The speed of sound in air is about 340 m/s at room temperature. Compare this with the speed of light, 3×10⁸ m/s. That is why you see lightning before you hear thunder. Sound can be reflected (echoes), refracted and diffracted, just like other waves.
writeBullets: Speed of sound: fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases
Solids — particles are closest together → vibrations pass on most efficiently
Speed in air ≈ 340 m/s. In water ≈ 1500 m/s. In steel ≈ 5000 m/s
Speed depends on the medium, not on the frequency or amplitude
Light travels much faster than sound. That is why you see lightning before you hear thunder

keyTerms.def: The rate at which sound travels through a medium; ~340 m/s in air at room temperature; faster in denser media

keyPoints.memTip: Solid > Liquid > Gas for sound speed. Particles closer together = faster passing on of vibrations.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Light slows down in denser media, but sound speeds up. These are easy to mix up. Remember the opposite relationship, and why: particle spacing and the forces between particles.

keyPoints.heading: Frequency, amplitude, pitch, and loudness
keyPoints.content: Two key properties of a sound wave decide how we hear it. Frequency → pitch: a higher frequency = a higher pitch. A piccolo makes high-frequency sound. A bass guitar makes low-frequency sound. Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz). Amplitude → loudness: a larger amplitude = a louder sound. A loud shout has a greater amplitude than a whisper. Loudness is measured indirectly in decibels (dB). The human hearing range is about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. - Below 20 Hz: infrasound. It is too low to hear. Earthquakes and whales make it. - Above 20,000 Hz: ultrasound. It is too high to hear. Bats and dolphins use it, and so do medicine and technology. These limits change with age. Older adults often cannot hear above 15,000–17,000 Hz.
writeBullets: Frequency → pitch: a higher frequency = a higher pitch
Amplitude → loudness: a larger amplitude = a louder sound
Human hearing range: 20 Hz – 20,000 Hz
Infrasound — below 20 Hz. Humans can't hear it (earthquakes, whales)
Ultrasound — above 20,000 Hz. Humans can't hear it. Used in medicine and sonar

keyTerms.def: The perceived highness or lowness of a sound; determined by frequency — higher frequency = higher pitch
The perceived volume of a sound; determined by amplitude — larger amplitude = louder
Sound below 20 Hz — below the human hearing threshold; produced by earthquakes and large animals
Sound above 20,000 Hz — above the human hearing threshold; used in medical imaging and sonar

keyPoints.memTip: FrEQ = pitch (Frequency → pitch). AMP = volume (AMPlitude → loudness).
keyPoints.tutor_note: It is easy to swap frequency and pitch, or amplitude and loudness. Use clear cause-and-effect wording: 'increasing frequency increases pitch'.

keyPoints.heading: Echoes, ultrasound, and sonar
keyPoints.content: An echo is a sound wave reflecting off a hard surface. You can use echo timing to work out distances: distance = speed × time. But remember the sound travels there and back. So the distance to the reflector = (speed × time) ÷ 2. Example: an echo returns after 0.4 s. The speed of sound = 340 m/s → total distance = 340 × 0.4 = 136 m → distance to the wall = 136 ÷ 2 = 68 m. Ultrasound (above 20,000 Hz) has important uses: - medical imaging: ultrasound pulses reflect off boundaries between tissues, such as between a baby and the fluid around it. The reflected pulses are used to build up an image. - sonar: ships send ultrasound pulses toward the seabed. They time the returning echo to measure the water depth. - industrial cleaning: high-frequency vibrations shake dirt loose. Ultrasound is used instead of X-rays for pregnancy scans because it does not ionise tissue. It is safe for the baby.
writeBullets: Echo — a sound wave reflecting off a hard surface
Distance = speed × time. But sound travels there AND back, so divide by 2
Ultrasound (>20,000 Hz) — medical imaging (pregnancy scans), sonar, industrial cleaning
Ultrasound is safer than X-rays. It is non-ionising, so it is used for pregnancy scans
Sonar — measures water depth or detects objects using timed ultrasound pulses

keyTerms.def: The reflection of a sound wave from a hard surface; used to calculate distances
Sound navigation and ranging — uses timed ultrasound pulses to measure distances underwater
Using reflected ultrasound pulses to build an image of internal structures (e.g. a foetus in the womb)

keyPoints.memTip: Echo distance = (speed × time) ÷ 2. Divide by 2 because the sound makes the return trip too. Ultrasound = safe scanning (no ionising radiation).
keyPoints.tutor_note: Echo questions almost always catch people who forget to halve. The wave travels to the reflector AND back. So halve the total distance, or the total time.

0.question: Why can't sound travel through a vacuum, such as outer space?
options: Sound is a mechanical wave that needs particles to vibrate. There are no particles in a vacuum
Sound travels too slowly to cross large distances
Sound waves are transverse and cannot pass through empty space
The frequency of sound is too low for it to travel without air resistance
0.correctFeedback: Exactly right! Sound needs a medium: particles to pass the vibrations along. A vacuum has no particles, so nothing can carry the wave.
0.wrongFeedback: Sound is a mechanical wave, so it needs a medium (particles) to travel. Electromagnetic waves, like light, can travel through a vacuum. Sound cannot, because there are no particles to vibrate.

1.question: A sound wave's frequency is increased, but its amplitude stays the same. How does this change the sound you hear?
options: The pitch increases but the loudness stays the same
The pitch and loudness both increase
The loudness increases but the pitch stays the same
The sound becomes quieter and higher
1.correctFeedback: Correct! Frequency controls pitch: a higher frequency = a higher pitch. Amplitude controls loudness. The amplitude is unchanged, so the loudness stays the same.
1.wrongFeedback: Remember: frequency → pitch, and amplitude → loudness. Changing the frequency only changes the pitch. The amplitude is unchanged, so the loudness stays the same.

3.question: A ship sends an ultrasound pulse downward. It gets the echo back 0.6 seconds later. The speed of sound in water is 1500 m/s. How deep is the water?
3.correctFeedback: Correct! Total distance = 1500 × 0.6 = 900 m. Divide by 2, because the sound travels to the bottom and back: 900 ÷ 2 = 450 m.
3.wrongFeedback: Use total distance = speed × time = 1500 × 0.6 = 900 m. Then halve it, because sound travels there AND back: 900 ÷ 2 = 450 m deep.

commonMistakes: Saying sound travels through a vacuum. Sound is a mechanical wave that needs particles to pass on vibrations. It cannot travel through empty space.
Forgetting to divide by 2 in echo and sonar calculations. The sound travels to the reflector and back. So you must halve the total distance (or the total time).
Mixing up frequency and amplitude. Frequency sets the pitch, not the loudness. Amplitude sets the loudness, not the pitch.

Saying sound travels fastest in gases because 'there's more room'. It is the opposite. Sound travels fastest in solids, because particles are closest together and the forces between them are strongest.
Describing ultrasound as a type of electromagnetic wave. Ultrasound is a sound wave (mechanical, longitudinal). It is not electromagnetic.
examTips: If asked why sound can't travel through a vacuum, always link it to the particle model. No particles means no medium for the vibrations to pass through.
In echo and sonar distance calculations, always write: distance to object = (speed × time) ÷ 2. Never forget the ÷ 2.
When comparing ultrasound and X-rays for medical imaging, say that ultrasound is non-ionising. This is the key safety advantage.
For questions on frequency and pitch, or amplitude and loudness, use exact exam wording. Say 'higher frequency produces a higher pitch'. Say 'greater amplitude produces a louder sound'.
The speed of sound in air ≈ 340 m/s. The question may give this value, or you may need to remember it. Check the question carefully.
